attacks.claim: Self-update trust chain relies on a single minisign key compiled into the binary with no documented rotation/revocation path, and no rollback protection; an attacker who can serve an older validly signed release (or a downgrade) via the GitHub Releases API can force users onto vulnerable versions, and --version vX.Y.Z accepts arbitrary tags.
attacks.evidence: "The minisign public key is compiled into the binary; the archive is rejected unless the signature verifies." and "--version vX.Y.Z" with no minimum-version or anti-downgrade check specified

attacks.claim: The plan trusts the GitHub API response to pick the latest tag and the archive URL without specifying that the download host, redirects, or tag/asset names are validated; the signature covers the archive but the plan does not say the .minisig is fetched from a trusted source or that the archive path is sanitised before writing.
attacks.evidence: "Queries the GitHub Releases API for the latest non-prerelease tag" and "Downloads the platform archive and its .minisig signature." with no host/path validation stated

attacks.claim: Self-update replaces the running executable in place; no statement that the new binary's permissions/ownership are preserved or that the temp file is created with safe perms, which matters when the binary lives in a shared path.
attacks.evidence: "Writes the new binary to a temp file in the same directory, fsyncs, then atomic rename over the current binary." — ABSENT: permission/ownership handling

attacks.claim: The persistent random install ID is a stable cross-run identifier tied to a user who opted in, and the plan does not state retention, deletion on opt-out, or whether it is rotated; combined with KVX version and OS/arch it is linkable over time at the collector.
attacks.evidence: "a random install ID generated locally" — ABSENT: rotation, deletion-on-off, retention of the ID server-side

attacks.claim: The collector sees source IP on every POST; the plan says raw events are discarded but does not say IPs are not logged or are truncated, contradicting the 'anonymous' framing in the prompt.
attacks.evidence: "writing daily aggregate counts only (raw events discarded after aggregation)" — ABSENT: handling of request IP/access logs

attacks.claim: Update discovery and telemetry depend on GitHub and a single donated VPS with no fallback or self-hosted collector option documented, so a provider outage or loss of the VPS silently disables both.
attacks.evidence: "on the project's existing donated VPS" — ABSENT: fallback or self-host instructions

attacks.claim: GitHub unauthenticated API rate limits (60 req/h per IP) can be exhausted by the startup notice check from shared NAT/CI runners, and the collector's load at 10-100x adoption is not estimated.
attacks.evidence: "a single HTTPS GET with a 1.5 s timeout" — ABSENT: rate-limit handling and collector capacity estimate

attacks.claim: The plan requires no paid infrastructure but the GitHub API and release-asset bandwidth for 14,000 weekly downloads plus update checks is not costed; the donated VPS has no stated capacity or egress budget.
attacks.evidence: "no new paid infrastructure" is a stated constraint; ABSENT: bandwidth/API budget math

attacks.claim: The atomic rename can leave kvx.prev and the active binary inconsistent if the process is interrupted between the two renames during rollback, and there is no described recovery; also no failure handling for a partially written kvx.prev.
attacks.evidence: "The previous binary is kept as kvx.prev; kvx self-update --rollback swaps them back." — ABSENT: crash-safety of the two-step swap

attacks.claim: Telemetry failures are dropped silently with no client-side observability, so the maintainers cannot detect collector outages before the monthly stats are published.
attacks.evidence: "failures are dropped, never retried in the foreground" — ABSENT: alerting on collector health

attacks.claim: Once shipped, the telemetry schema and the install-ID mechanism cannot be cleanly withdrawn from users' machines in older versions; the plan has no sunset/kill-switch that works on versions already installed beyond the KVX_TELEMETRY env var, and self-update on old versions may not reach a version that disables it.
attacks.evidence: "KVX_TELEMETRY=0 hard-disables regardless of config." — ABSENT: remote kill-switch or forced-off path for shipped clients

attacks.claim: The 24 h notice is stated as 'at most once per 24 h' but no persistence location or clock/timezone handling is specified; also the consent prompt is 'once' but no state is defined if the user answers in a non-interactive session that never prompts.
attacks.evidence: "at most once per 24 h" and "asks once: ... Empty answer = no." — ABSENT: where the last-check timestamp and consent state are stored

attacks.claim: The motivating claim that 41% of downloads on old versions is a problem is stated from per-asset download counts, but download counts include mirrors, CI caches and package-manager re-downloads, so the 41% figure does not establish that users are on vulnerable or stale installs; the success target of 59%→75% is then built on this unvalidated baseline.
attacks.evidence: "41% of release-asset downloads 60 days later were still for versions <= v2.6.2 (GitHub release download counts, tallied per asset)." and "(from 59%)"

attacks.claim: The 59% baseline in success measures conflicts with the 41% stale-download figure in motivation without explanation (59% latest-or-newer vs 41% old is consistent only if the 'latest minor' definition is the same; it is not defined).
attacks.evidence: "share of downloads on the latest minor version >= 75% (from 59%)" vs "41% ... still for versions <= v2.6.2"

attacks.claim: Telemetry collection of OS/arch, version and command usage from EU/UK users is personal data under GDPR when linked to a persistent install ID; the plan gives no lawful-basis statement, DPA/controller identity, or data-subject deletion path, and the consent prompt text is not reviewed for adequacy.
attacks.evidence: "Share anonymous usage stats ... Empty answer = no." — ABSENT: legal basis, controller identity, deletion-request process

attacks.claim: The one-time consent prompt and the startup notice are single-line stderr/TTY text with no stated screen-reader or non-color guidance; the prompt's default-no convention is not explained for assistive users.
attacks.evidence: "Share anonymous usage stats (...)? [y/N]" — ABSENT: accessibility review

attacks.claim: Users in package-manager installs receive a refusal rather than an update path, and the consent prompt appears on the first interactive run after upgrade, adding friction to a common command.
attacks.evidence: "self-update refuses and prints the matching brew/apt/dnf command" and "On first interactive run after upgrade, kvx asks once"

attacks.claim: Telemetry and self-update are both bundled into one 3-week, 2-maintainer build with a release-candidate week that leaves little slack; the collector is a separate service the plan does not assign to an owner or test.
attacks.evidence: "Week 3: collector service, docs/telemetry.md, release notes, v2.8.0-rc1 for 1 week, then v2.8.0." — ABSENT: collector owner and tests

attacks.claim: The 'two security fixes this year had slow uptake' motivation is cited, but the plan does not state a deprecation or minimum-supported-version policy, so self-update alone does not address the stated security-uptake problem.
attacks.evidence: "Maintainers want users on current versions (two security fixes this year had slow uptake)" — ABSENT: minimum-supported-version policy
